name: Full-bottomed wig

card.summary: A long periwig of the late 17th and 18th centuries that covered the back and shoulders, worn to add imposing hair volume and to cover baldness.
card.note: Historically heavy and costly; today worn mainly in some courts and ceremonies.

quick.overview:
The full-bottomed wig was a luxurious men's periwig of the late 1600s that flowed over the back, shoulders and chest. Wearers used it to give themselves a full head of hair and a status-signalling silhouette, and wigs also concealed baldness and helped reduce head lice.

Wigs spread through Europe in the 1660s, fell out of everyday fashion by about 1765 and effectively ended with the hair powder tax of 1795. Full-bottomed wigs survive in ceremonial dress for judges and senior barristers in some countries.
quick.how: Wigs were made by perruquiers, who measured the head and built a net foundation. Hair was sewn on silk wefts, the oldest method, and ventilated hand-knotting came in the 19th century. Human hair made the finest wigs, with horse and goat hair as cheaper options.
quick.risks: Elaborate 17th-century wigs were expensive and often heavy and uncomfortable. They were also associated with lice control because the natural hair underneath was shaved or cropped.

lead: The full-bottomed wig is a long periwig that covers the back and shoulders and flows down the chest, fashionable in the late 17th century. [1] Men of rank, courtiers and military officers wore it to present a full, imposing head of hair, and wigs more generally served to disguise baldness and reduce head lice. [2]

Louis XIII began wearing a wig in 1624 after going bald, and his son Louis XIV helped spread the fashion across Europe in the 1660s. Charles II brought periwigs to England on his restoration in 1660. [2]
Full-bottomed wigs are still worn in ceremonial dress by judges and senior barristers in some Commonwealth jurisdictions. [1]

angle.text: The wig gave the wearer long, full hair regardless of his own, covering baldness and signalling rank. The effect lasted only while it was worn.

paras: The style covered the back and shoulders and flowed down the chest. [1] Officers in European armies wore full-bottomed, natural-coloured wigs in the late 1600s, while ordinary soldiers usually greased and powdered their own hair. [2]

Wigs returned in the 16th and 17th centuries to compensate for hair loss and reduce lice. [2] France formed a wigmakers' guild in 1665. Men later powdered wigs white or off-white. Wig-wearing fell out of fashion by 1765, revived in the 1770s, and the 1795 Duty on Hair Powder Act effectively ended the fashion. [2] Bishops of the Church of England and Church of Ireland wore ceremonial wigs until 1832. [1]

Perruquiers measured the head and built a block form. In the weft method hair is sewn to silk threads and attached to a net foundation; ventilated hand-knotting was introduced in the 19th century. [2] The best wigs used human hair, with horse and goat hair cheaper; elaborate wigs were costly and heavy. [1]
Judges and senior barristers wear full-bottomed wigs on ceremonial occasions. [1]
